headlines.article_text: Wayfair (W) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Wayfair said its sales jumped 10% in the third quarter as the retailer posted its strongest quarter since the pandemic. The company also reported double-digit revenue growth in the U.S. CFO Kate Gulliver told CNBC the growth is largely due to the company continuing to take market share in what's been a sluggish housing market. In this article W Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Cheng Xin | Getty Images Wayfair on Wednesday said it posted its strongest quarter of sales growth since the pandemic as the furniture retailer continues to win over customers and take market share. The company said it saw double-digit revenue growth in the U.S., reaching about $3 billion, an 11.4% increase from the year prior. Still, international net revenue for the quarter decreased 2.3% year over year to $380 million. Wayfair's stock jumped about 10% on Wednesday. The report comes as the housing market remains sluggish. But the furniture and home goods retailer has reported consistent growth over the past year. CFO Kate Gulliver told CNBC that Wayfair's momentum is building as it takes market share. "We see the overall consumer in the U.S. in this category, we think it's roughly flattish, and so that's our [market] share momentum continuing to build," Gulliver said. She added that shopper loyalty, the opening of new stores, the company's luxury furniture business and an emphasis on value has allowed Wayfair to win more consumers. Customers are also continuing to spend, whether at the company's value prices or on the luxury side, she added. "We've been highly promotional for the last few years, and the promotional activity this year is actually very consistent with last year," she said. "It maintains this sort of momentum on promotional activity this year." Here's how the company performed in its third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 93 cents adjusted vs. 79 cents expected Revenue: $3.42 billion vs. $3.38 billion expected For the period ended Sept. 30, Wayfair reported net income of $62 million, or 45 cents per share, compared with a loss of $99 million, or 76 cents per share, the year prior. Total revenue grew 9.7% year over year, reaching $3.42 billion. The company said its active customers grew 4.7% year over year, reaching 22.2 million. It also saw a 12.2% increase in orders delivered during the quarter to about 11 million. As the company looks ahead to the holiday season and the fourth quarter, Gulliver said it's maintaining promotional activity similar to last year. She added that Wayfair is confident that its range of prices and products will appeal to a broad base of consumers. "We've seen that growth play out," Gulliver said. "We've seen that flow through to EBITDA, ultimately to net income positive this quarter, which is really another key piece in the story and the momentum here, so we feel very good about the quarter of the performance." CVS in 2024 considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea. Mario Tama | Getty Images CVS Health plans to break itself up — and this time, the bet looks a lot more viable. The healthcare conglomerate on Wednesday announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. CVS would separate its pharmacy business – including roughly 9,000 retail locations – from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark. The move comes more than two years after CVS considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea. At the time, analysts questioned whether the retail pharmacy business could survive on its own. “Back then, the idea of retail standing alone was unthinkable,” Brian Tanquilut, senior equity research analyst at Jefferies, told CNBC. But the economics of the businesses have changed: CVS's retail pharmacy business has become more consistently profitable, while its insurer, Aetna, has improved its performance despite persistently high medical costs in Medicare Advantage plans. That could make it easier for the company to separate the units — and for investors to recognize the value of each on its own, rather than valuing them together as one sprawling healthcare conglomerate. “For us, it's showing the stability of the pharmacy,” Michael Cherny, senior research analyst at Leerink Partners, said in an interview. “This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome.” CVS CEO David Joyner told CNBC’s "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that back in 2024, the company was "in a turnaround" without the flexibility, cash or business performance to execute a split. Now, CVS has posted eight consecutive quarters of beating Wall Street earnings estimates and has raised its guidance several times over the last two years, thanks to improvement across its PBM, pharmacy and insurer. Since taking the helm in 2024, Joyner has pursued an aggressive turnaround plan that involves $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs. The company also now expects to generate at least $15.5 billion in operating cash flow in 2026, a roughly 70% increase from $9.1 billion in 2024, and says it has reached its leverage target ahead of schedule. "What's changed in two years is the fact that we now can look at this business and the assets that are assembled and really determine, without any distress or without anything that we have to do, what is the right strategic decision to make," Joyner told analysts on a call Wednesday, adding that the decision comes "out of strength." While investors have largely cheered CVS's progress in recent years, Wall Street appeared more pessimistic about Wednesday's announcement, as the company's shares dropped about 12%. That’s created opportunities for CVS to gain market share, some analysts told CNBC. CVS has also introduced changes to its pharmacy reimbursement model. Its CostVantage program is designed to replace the traditional process with a more transparent, cost-based model. Some analysts say that has helped the company better align reimbursement with the cost of dispensing prescriptions and contributed to steadier profits. Those developments represent a meaningful shift for a business that has faced years of pressure from declining prescription reimbursement, store closures and competition from online pharmacies and other retailers. That doesn't mean the retail pharmacy has become a high-growth business. CVS's retail pharmacy segment remains a relatively low-margin operation, with adjusted operating margins of roughly 4% to 5%. But analysts say it may now be stable and profitable enough to operate independently – even if investors value it at a discount to CVS's other businesses. In a note Wednesday, RBC Capital Markets analyst Ben Hendrix said the lower valuation investors assign to the retail pharmacy unit has weighed on CVS's overall value and obscured the earnings strength of businesses like Aetna and Caremark. The underlying growth of the insurance and PBM businesses is also stronger than that of retail pharmacy, Tanquilut said, after accounting for changes to Caremark's rebate arrangements. Aetna in particular has gotten a better handle on medical costs by exiting unprofitable markets, expanding value-based care models, and tightening utilization management. Regulatory headwinds The breakup also comes as Caremark faces mounting scrutiny over PBM practices, including state-level legal and regulatory challenges involving the businesses and their relationships with pharmacies. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban any one company from owning both a pharmacy and a PBM — thought the Arkansas measure has been held up in court. Cherny noted that legal hurdles involving PBMs in other states have continued to pile up. “Through what seems to be a never-ending litany of state lawsuits, it feels like it's been under more pressure,” Cherny said. “It's unclear if it just became, for lack of a better term, too tenuous to move forward with those two entities combined as one. I’m not sure.” The exterior of a CVS pharmacy store is seen on August 07, 2024 in Austin, Texas. Brandon Bell | Getty Images Even so, Joyner told the Wall Street Journal that the company wasn’t splitting up because of regulatory issues. CVS has said the separation follows a strategic review and is intended to give each business greater focus and flexibility. The move also marks a significant departure from the integrated healthcare strategy CVS spent years building. CVS spent roughly $70 billion to acquire Aetna in 2018 and argued that combining health insurance, pharmacy benefit management, retail pharmacies and health providers under one roof would help coordinate care and create a competitive advantage. CVS was still promoting that model as recently as its investor day last year. The proposed split suggests the company now sees more value in separating at least some of those businesses – though it is not abandoning vertical integration altogether. The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount. "In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement. McDonald's same-store sales returned to growth in September after falling in July and August, CFO Ian Borden said on the company's earnings conference call. However, in response to an analyst question, he clarified that he did not say that U.S. same-store sales would be better in the fourth quarter. Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years. To reverse same-store sales declines, McDonald's focused its marketing on its Extra Value Meals and restarted regional and national promotions on its mobile app, which are important to its most frequent diners. As McDonald's tries to regain its footing in the U.S., the chain is also testing two new value menus, one with mix and match bundles and the other with set combinations of menu items, executives said on the earnings call. The offering that resonates the most with customers and franchisees will be rolled out across the U.S. in early 2027. Shares of the company rose about 6% in afternoon trading. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.57 adjusted vs. $3.38 expected Revenue: $7.16 billion vs. $7.29 billion expected The company reported third-quarter net income of $2.49 billion, or $3.51 per share, up from $2.28 billion, or $3.18 per share, a year earlier. Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share. Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion. The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount. McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount. "In the majority of our large international markets, we're holding or gaining share," Borden said on the company's conference call. "It's a soft consumer environment, but we're doing well." France was a weak spot, McDonald's said. Kempczinski said that franchisees in France recently voted on a strategy to turn the business around. headlines.title: Hyperscalers and Apple surge after election results remove investor uncertainty
headlines.summary: Apple, Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft stock was up after the midterms, while stocks tied to Trump advisor Elon Musk and data centers fell on Wednesday.
headlines.article_text: Apple and other big tech stocks surge after 2026 midterm elections Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Many of the biggest technology companies are surging on Wednesday, after Democrats scored a seismic victory in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate. Tuesday's election results remove uncertainty in the market, David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said on "Squawk on the Street." Many of the technology stocks rising on Wednesday are what are known as hyperscalers, and analysts say they are poised to benefit from increased regulation. In this article GOOGL MSFT META AMZN AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Apple's new CEO John Ternus holds the new iPhone 18 as he attends iPhone launch day at the Apple Fifth Avenue store in New York City on September 18, 2026, for the debut of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Timothy A. Clary | Afp | Getty Images Many of the biggest technology companies are surging on Wednesday, after Democrats scored a seismic victory in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate. During trading on Wednesday, Amazon surged 8%, Google rose over 6%, Microsoft rose 4%, Meta was up 3%, and Apple — which faced Trump's tariffs and recently got refunds — climbed nearly 7%. Tuesday's results remove uncertainty in the market, David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said on "Squawk on the Street." He said the divided government would lead to "moderation in growth, moderation in inflation, less uncertainty, and I think that's all helping the stock market move up today." However, some stocks, particularly those tied to Trump advisor Elon Musk as well as the AI data center buildout, fell on Wednesday. As results came in last night, some observers saw bad news for big technology companies because of their bets to build large AI-focused data centers. There were 41 local ballot measures on Tuesday to place restrictions or clear the way for AI data centers, and voters sided against data centers in 40 of them. In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their voting decision. Analysts said that Democrats who proposed data center moratoriums won gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, raising fears that projects could get snarled in regulation or blocked by politicians. "Recall that backup power emissions, zoning, water, interconnect/grid, and tax considerations are often overseen by state regulators," Macquarie analyst Paul Golding said in a note on Wednesday. Tesla stock fell 2%, and SpaceX was down 3%. Nvidia, which makes the chips for most of these AI data center projects, slipped just over 1%. Many of the technology stocks rising on Wednesday are what are known as hyperscalers, or the largest cloud providers that also pair massive capex spending with robust free cash flow and have the most experience and capability to construct AI data centers. "We believe higher regulatory barriers entrench incumbents, and increase risks (and raise required ROICs) for new entrants," wrote Needham analyst Laura Martin in a note on Wednesday. "Hyperscalers are AI incumbents." Smaller AI cloud providers, often called neoclouds, got whacked on Wednesday. CoreWeave stock fell 10%. Baird analysts said in a note that the election results create a "sentiment headwind" for neoclouds. Golding, the Macquarie analyst, wrote that he remains bullish on AI infrastructure, and that well-capitalized, high-quality operators stand to benefit the most if projects in some states slow down. "Neoclouds may pay more to lease powered shells for GPUaaS commitments (and pass on costs), while hyperscaler/AI lab capacity needs could intensify competition for even more limited supply," Golding wrote. Tuesday's results could signal restrictions on new data center developments in some states, but it doesn't necessarily signal a nationwide slowdown in construction, Chris Miglino, CEO of Axe Compute , said in an email. Companies are still raising capital, enterprises are spending, and there's still a need for more capacity. Miglino said that increased regulation in some regions could cause investors and customers to look more closely at different cloud computing providers, and opt for those with the capability to deliver capacity, or which offer AI inference to a specific industry niche. "If you've already secured power, have the financing in place and understand how to deploy and operate compute infrastructure efficiently, you're in a much stronger position than a company that's still trying to figure those things out," Miglino said. headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CoreWeave, Micron, Booking Holdings, McDonald's, CVS Health & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CRWV, MU, BKNG, MCD, CVS Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. AI infrastructure — Companies tied to data centers slid following Democrats' midterm election victories as traders prepared for a slowdown in the buildout effort . The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) slid more than 2%. Shares of Comfort Systems and Vistra tumbled 17% and 13%, respectively. Memory stocks Micron and Sandisk lost 5% and 7%. Defense stocks — Shares of defense companies tumbled after Democrats swept Congress in the midterm elections. The iShares U.S. Aerospace & Defense ETF (ITA) slipped more than 1%; Lockheed Martin 's stock fell 6%. Shares of Howmet Aerospace and Northrop Grumman lost more than 4%. Trump Media & Technology Group — Shares of President Donald Trump 's social media and tech company were down 11% after a decisive victory by Democrats in the midterms Tuesday night. Trump owns 41% of the company, which owns social media platform Truth Social. Democrats taking control of Congress add a check on the president's policies. Tesla , SpaceX — Shares of Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX dropped 3% each. The moves come after the Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Many of the newly elected candidates have criticized the rapid data center buildout that's been fueled by artificial intelligence. SpaceX operates an AI supercomputing infrastructure in Tennessee and Mississippi , while Tesla has one in Texas. Neocloud stocks — Shares of so-called neocloud companies moved lower, with CoreWeave 's stock dropping 9%, shares of Iren tumbling 11% and shares of Nebius slipping about 6%. The Democratic wins in Texas and rejection of data centers in ballots across the country are expected to create hurdles for data center plays. Trimble — The software company's stock tanked almost 18%. Trimble said it anticipates organic annual recurring revenue growth of roughly 10% for 2026, down from its previous call for a range of 12% to 14%. Fidelity National Information Services — The financial software stock tumbled 24% after the company slashed its full-year earnings outlook. FIS sees adjusted earnings per share in a range of $5.82 to $5.89. That's down from a prior forecast of $6.15 per share to $6.24 per share. AppLovin — Shares rallied more than 10% as traders awaited the company's third-quarter results after the bell Wednesday. Analysts polled by FactSet expected AppLovin to report earnings per share of $4.03 on revenue of $2.075 billion. Clear Secure — Shares soared 33% after the identity verification company lifted its forecast for free cash flow for the full year. Clear Secure sees at least $490 million in free cash flow, topping the FactSet consensus estimate of $482.9 million. Third-quarter results also topped the Street's estimates. Consumer discretionary stocks — Cyclical stocks that sell to consumers rallied after better-than-expected results from Booking Holdings . Shares of Booking and Expedia jumped 11% and 13%, respectively. Nike 's stock rallied more than 6%, and shares of Amazon climbed almost 7%. Novo Nordisk — Shares gained over 6% after the global healthcare company reported earnings of 5.79 Danish kroner, or about 63 cents per share, compared with Wall Street expectations of 5.10 kroner, or about 55 cents. The company raised its fiscal 2026 outlook, citing expectations for GLP-1 product sales. McDonald's — The fast-food restaurant chain reported mixed quarterly results , sending shares 5% higher. Adjusted earnings came in at $3.57 per share, topping the $3.38 expected from analysts polled by LSEG. However, its revenue of $7.16 billion fell short of the $7.29 billion consensus estimate. CVS Health — Shares fell more than 12% after the company said it would split into two separate publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. The move would reverse CVS' $78 billion acquisition of Aetna and separate the company's retail pharmacy business. Duolingo — Shares surged 32% after the language learning software company reported third-quarter revenue of $309 million. That topped an LSEG consensus of $303 million. Monthly active users totaled 153 million for the quarter, exceeding a 149 million forecast. Adjusted EBITDA margin also topped expectations. Block — The fintech stock rallied almost 16% after Block posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that exceeded expectations, and raised guidance for the full year ending December. Adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share topped the $1.03 LSEG consensus estimate, while revenue of $6.72 billion beat the $6.59 billion consensus. Renewable energy stocks — Shares of renewable energy companies moved higher after the Democratic sweep of Congress. Shares of Sunrun and Plug Power each climbed roughly 7%, while shares of Nextpower jumped 15%. Datadog — The cloud monitoring company saw shares sink 14% after it released its third-quarter financial results. While it beat on both the top and bottom lines, its revenue guidance came in soft. Datadog expects revenue of $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion for the fourth quarter, versus the $1.20 billion consensus estimate. Kraft Heinz — The food and beverage manufacturer's stock gained 6%. Kraft Heinz said it will divest its North America coffee business to One Rock Capital Partners. The company also reported adjusted earnings of 53 cents per share on revenue of $6.12 billion for its third quarter, topping expectations. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected EPS of 42 cents on revenue of $6.09 billion. — CNBC's Darla Mercado, Deena Zaidi, Paulina Likos, Sarah Min, Davis Giangiulio, Ananya Chetia, Fred Imbert, Scott Schnipper and Nick Wells contributed reporting.
